articleHeadline: Africa: Mosquitoes Carrying Malaria Are Evolving More Quickly Than Insecticides Can Kill Them - Researchers Pinpoint How
articleSummary: Malaria kills more than 600,000 people annually. Environmental exposure, including agricultural insecticides, may fuel evolution, underscoring the need for more sophisticated vector control, including gene-drive trials.

Public health response focuses on enhanced surveillance, genomic sequencing, and entry-point monitoring; widespread vaccination and prior infections in India contribute to population immunity. Guidelines remain: stay up-to-date with vaccines, maintain hygiene, avoid crowded places during outbreaks; vulnerable groups should remain cautious. Ongoing global sequencing and epidemiological studies will determine Cicada’s transmissibility and whether it could outcompete existing strains, but current threat assessment remains low.

York researchers identify ESB2, a protein inside the parasite’s Expression Site Body, acting as a molecular shredder that destroys parts of its genetic instructions as they are printed, selectively removing helper genes while leaving cloak directives intact. This real-time redaction explains why the parasite overproduces cloak proteins yet suppresses immune-detectable components, enabling stealth in the human host and possibly opening new treatment avenues. The finding, published in Nature Microbiology, comes from University of York work led by Dr. Joana Faria with Lianne Lansink as first author, and is supported by the Sir Henry Dale Fellowship (Wellcome Trust/Royal Society) with international collaboration across the UK, Portugal, the Netherlands, Germany, Singapore and Brazil. Transmission by tsetse fly; untreated disease invades the CNS causing sleep disruption, confusion, and coma.

articleSummary: Indonesia’s Ministry of Health issued a circular alerting medical personnel and health workers to heightened vigilance for measles (campak) and to prevent transmission amid rising cases among health staff. articleSummary: Hospital Estadual de Doenças Tropicais Dr. Anuar Auad (HDT) in Goiás, Brazil, hosted the International Conference on Histoplasmosis—Diagnostic Gaps, Global Burden, and the Role of Endemic Centers in Strategic Responses. The event highlighted HDT’s leadership, noting it accounts for about 41% of histoplasmosis cases studied in Brazil. Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, an opportunistic disease especially in people living with HIV, transplant recipients, and other immunosuppressed patients; disseminated disease is among the most frequent opportunistic infections in HIV/AIDS in the Americas, with untreated mortality exceeding 90%. Diagnosis remains challenging and delays treatment. Highlights included the HISTO-FACT and Induction studies, underpinning a new seven-year international protocol. HDT is a reference center for infectious diseases and dermatology in Goiás and is accredited ONA 3; the hospital operates under Instituto Sócrates Guanaes (ISG).

articleSummary: Minas Gerais expands chikungunya vaccination to Uberlândia and Araguari in the Triângulo Mineiro starting 31 March 2026, aiming for at least 50% coverage among residents 18–59 years old. articleSummary: Chikungunya outbreak in Dourados, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, driven by Aedes aegypti. By 30 March 2026, Dourados reports 1,035 confirmed cases, 943 under investigation, and 354 discarded (positivity 74.5%). Ten new cases in the last 24 hours; 33 hospitalized. No new deaths in the latest hours. The city remains under a 90-day public-health emergency declared on 27 March; a prior decree covered Greater Dourados. The Ministry of Health has allocated R$900,000 to strengthen surveillance, vector control, and care.
